sentences.text: This is a suit filed by the plaintiffs seeking possession, arrears of rent, mesne profits, and permanent injunction in respect of property bearing House No. 34, Malikpur, Delhi-110009.

Plaintiff's version 1. Brief facts of the present case as per plaint are that :-
(a) Plaintiffs have filed the present suit stating interalia that they are absolute joint owners of H No. 34, Malikpur, Delhi 110009 (hereinafter be referred to as suit property).
The defendant was inducted by plaintiff no.2 as tenant for a period of three years for a monthly rent of Rs.4,000/- at the suit property.
At the time of inducting defendant as tenant, she informed the plaintiffs that she is single unmarried lady and is earning her livelihood from physiotherapy being a physiotherapist.

It is further averred that in February, 2013, plaintiff no.2 received calls from neighbours about unusual conduct of defendant wherein she had permitted a middle aged man to reside with her at the tenanted premises.
Being confronted with the defendant

,
plaintiff no.2 was informed that the said man namely Sh Sanjay Singh is her fiance and due to social restrictions, she had not revealed her relations with him.

(b) It is further averred that plaintiff no.2, in September, 2013, came to know that defendant lodged an FIR against her fiance Sh Sanjay Singh with PS Mukherjee Nagar, Delhi u/s 498A/406/506/ 376 IPC.

Arguments 9. I have heard the final arguments advanced by Ld. counsels for the parties and have perused the entire record.
9.1

It is argued by learned counsel for the plaintiffs that the defendant was inducted as tenant in the suit property by plaintiff no.2 at a monthly rent of 4,000, that she defaulted in payment of rent from September 2013, and that despite service of legal notice dated 25.07.2014 terminating tenancy she failed to vacate.

It is submitted that PW-1's testimony, supported by site plan, legal notice, and postal receipt, has remained unrebutted as no cross- examination was conducted, and therefore must be accepted as true.

The plaintiffs contend that once landlord-tenant relationship is established, the tenant is estopped under Section 116 of the Evidence Act from disputing the landlord's title, and hence they are entitled to possession, arrears of rent, mesne profits, and injunction.
9.2

Per Contra, it is argued by learned counsel for the defendant that the plaintiffs have failed to establish their ownership and title over the suit property, and that weakness of the defence cannot absolve the plaintiffs of their duty to prove their own case.

It is submitted that the defendant was tenant under Sahib Singh Kohli at a rent of 1,500 per month, and that a security deposit of NITISH KUMAR NITISH KUMAR SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.06 17:14:02 +0530 CS SCJ No.

10. I have heard the rival contentions advanced by Ld. Counsel for the parties and have perused the material on record.

My findings on the issues are as under:
11. Issue no.1 & 5 1.
Whether the plaintiff is entitled to the decree of possession of suit property as prayed for?

sentences.text: Whether the suit filed by plaintiff is barred by Section 50 of Delhi Rent Control Act ? OPD 12.
The onus to prove issue no.1 was upon the plaintiff and the onus to prove issue no.5 was upon the defendant.
It is pertinent to mention that the plaintiffs have alleged that the defendant was tenant in the suit property and plaintiff no.2 was the landlord and that the rate of rent was Rs 4,000/ per month.
It is alleged that despite service of notice to vacate, the defendant has failed to comply.
The primary defence of the defendant is that she was not tenant of plaintiff number 2 but of one Sahib Singh Kohli and that rate of rent was Rs 1500/ month.

In order to prove his case, plaintiffs examined plaintiff no.2 as PW-1 and he categorically deposed that the defendant was inducted as tenant in the suit property at a monthly rent of 4,000,
and that despite service of legal notice dated 25.07.2014 terminating tenancy, the defendant failed to vacate.
He exhibited the site plan, the legal notice, and the postal receipt evidencing dispatch.
Significantly, PW-1 was not subjected to any cross- examination despite repeated opportunities.

14. It is beneficial to herein to refer to Muddasani Venkata Narsaiah v. Muddasani Sarojana, AIR 2016 SC 2250 , wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has held that if a witness's testimony is not subjected to cross-examination on material facts, such testimony remains unchallenged and must ordinarily be accepted as true.

entities.text: Muddasani Venkata Narsaiah v. Muddasani Sarojana, AIR 2016 SC 2250
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It was emphasized that cross-examination is the primary tool to test veracity, and failure to exercise it amounts to acceptance of the witness's version.
15.
Applying this principle, the testimony of PW-1 must be accepted as true.
His deposition as regards landlordship, induction of defendant as tenant, rent at 4,000, and termination of tenancy stands unrebutted and unchallenged.

The plaintiffs have therefore discharged their burden under issue no. 1.
16.

The defendant's primary defence was that she was tenant under one Sahib Singh Kohli at a rent of 1,500 per month, and therefore the suit is barred under Section 50 of the Delhi Rent NITISH NITISH KUMAR Control Act.

However, DW-1's testimony is riddled with contradictions which makes the same unreliable.

In her examination-in-chief, she claimed that a receipt for 2,00,000 security deposit was with Sh.
Sanjay Singh, but in cross-examination she stated that no such receipt was prepared.
She further stated that she did not know if Sahib Singh Kohli was son of plaintiff no.2, yet affirmed the suggestion that she lodged an FIR against Sahib Singh Kohli, son of Sunny Kohli.
These contradictions strike at the root of her defence and render her testimony unreliable.

The plea of tenancy under Sahib Singh Kohli at 1,500 per month is unsupported by any documentary Joginder Kohli Anr vs Neetu Singh on 6 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/9051238/

sentences.text: It is noteworthy that defendant admitted that one FIR i.e. Ex DW1/P1 was got lodged by her against the plaintiffs and Sahib Singh Kohli.
The mention of plaintiff number 2 therein in the FIR as landlord also gives credence to the version of plaintiffs.

Though, it was argued that mere marking the document as Exhibit would not amount to its proof, it is noteworthy that the defendant in her cross-examination did not state anything with respect to the complaint forming basis of FIR.
18. It is also noteworthy that the defendant herself has mentioned about the said FIR against plaintiffs and Sahib Kohli in her written statement but she did not file copy of it on record.

Such suppression also indicates that the defendant has deliberately withheld material evidence which could have clarified the nature of NITISH Digitally signed by NITISH KUMAR SHARMA KUMAR Date: 2025.12.06 SHARMA 17:14:17 +0530 CS SCJ No. 535476/2016 Joginder Kohli and Anr. sentences.text: When a party refers to a document in pleadings but fails to produce it, the court is entitled to draw an adverse inference under Section 114(g) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
The defendant's omission to place the FIR on record, despite relying upon it in her written statement, suggests that its contents would not have supported her defence.

On the contrary, her admission in cross-examination that she lodged the FIR against plaintiff no.2 and Sahib Singh Kohli, and it is forthcoming from such copy that plaintiff no.2 was described therein as landlord, lends corroboration to the plaintiffs' version of landlordship and tenancy.

19. It was argued by learned counsel for the defendant that the plaintiffs have failed to establish their title over the suit property, and that weakness of the defendant's case would not absolve the plaintiffs of their duty to prove their own case.
This argument is well-founded in principle, for it is trite law that the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of his own case and not on the weakness of the defence.

However, in the considered opinion of this court, the plaintiffs were not required to prove their title to the property once it is proved that defendant was tenant under plaintiff no.2.
20.

It is no gainsay that as per Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, once the relationship of landlord and tenant is established, the tenant is estopped from challenging the title of the landlord at the commencement of tenancy.
The defendant's plea of tenancy under Sahib Singh Kohli is unsupported by any document.

It is also contended by Ld. Counsel for defendant that the site plan of the suit property is incorrect and the said document has not been proved as per law.
However, it is to be noted that no such objection qua the mode of proof was taken at the time of tendering of the document and as the said objection is untenable.
Even otherwise, there is no counter site plan filed by defendant and no cross-examination has been done on behalf of defendant qua the site plan.
Further, DW-1 in her cross-examination has clarified that there is only one room alongwith one store and kitchen, thereby strengthening the case of plaintiff.
Thus, the contention of the defendant has to be rejected.
21. As regards issue No. 5, the burden was upon the defendant to establish that the suit is barred under Section 50 of the Delhi Rent Control Act.
However, the defendant has failed to discharge this burden.
Her plea of rent at 1,500 per month is unsupported by any documentary evidence. PW-1's unrebutted testimony has established that rent was fixed at 4,000 per month.
Further, the defendant has not placed on record any notification to show that the suit property is covered by the Rent Control Act or by any slum area notification.

It is settled that mere assertion in pleadings,
without proof, cannot oust the jurisdiction of the civil court.
Therefore, the plea of bar under Section 50 of Delhi Rent Control Act is rejected.

The plaintiffs have also proved by way of unrebutted testimony of PW-1 that defendant has not paid rent since September 2013 and was thus in arrears of rent till July 2014.

The defendant, though stated in her examination as DW-1 that rent was paid to Sahib Singh Kohli and that an amount of Rs 2,00,000/ is deposited as security with Sahib Singh Kohli- the same remained a bald assertion as no documentary evidence was brought for the same and rather contradictory statements made regarding the security deposit, makes the claim of defendant unreliable.
Issue no. 2 accordingly stands decided in favour of the plaintiff.
28. As regards mesne profits, the plaintiffs have claimed damages at the rate of 2,000 per day for unauthorized occupation after termination of tenancy.
Once tenancy is validly terminated, the defendant's continued occupation is unauthorized, and the plaintiffs are entitled to mesne profits for use and occupation.
However, the quantum of mesne profits have to be determined on a reasonable basis.
While the plaintiffs claimed 2,000 per day (amounting to 60,000 per month), no independent market evidence was produced to substantiate this figure.
As per Ex. PW2/A, a rent agreement of another tenant, Ms. Bhawna Jhorar, rate of rent at 4,500 per month in 2012-2013 indicates that the prevailing market rent was higher than the contractual 4,000.
Though this supports entitlement of plaintiffs to an enhanced rate, but not to the extent of 60,000 per month.

Whether the suit filed by plaintiff is liable to be dismissed for want of cause of action ? OPD 31.
The onus qua this issue was upon the defendant.
It has been argued that the suit of the plaintiffs is liable to be dismissed as plaintiffs have failed to prove their title to the suit property.

Ld. Counsel for the defendant relied on Smriti Debbarma v Sri Prabha Ranjan Debbarma 2022 Joginder Kohli Anr vs Neetu Singh on 6 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/9051238/

32. In the humble opinion of this court, the reliance of defendant on the aforesaid judgments is misplaced as the plaintiffs herein have claimed possession from the defendant by asserting that defendant was tenant of plaintiff no.2.
In a suit between landlord and tenant, plaintiff is not required to prove title if he is able to establish landlord-tenant relationship.

33. In view of the findings on issue no.1, it is clear that the plaintiffs have been successful in establishing that the plaintiff no.2 was the landlord of the suit property and defendant was the tenant.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
His deposition as regards landlordship, induction of defendant as tenant, rent at 4,000, and termination of tenancy stands unrebutted and unchallenged.
The plaintiffs have therefore discharged their burden under issue no. 1.
16.
The defendant's primary defence was that she was tenant under one Sahib Singh Kohli at a rent of 1,500 per month, and therefore the suit is barred under Section 50 of the Delhi Rent NITISH NITISH KUMAR Control Act.
When a party refers to a document in pleadings but fails to produce it, the court is entitled to draw an adverse inference under Section 114(g) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
It is no gainsay that as per Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, once the relationship of landlord and tenant is established, the tenant is estopped from challenging the title of the landlord at the commencement of tenancy.
The defendant's plea of tenancy under Sahib Singh Kohli is unsupported by any document.
As per Section 108 (q) of TPA, a lessee is under obligation to vacate the tenanted property and hand over the possession to landlord/lessor on termination of tenancy.
However, the defendant has failed to discharge this burden.
Her plea of rent at 1,500 per month is unsupported by any documentary evidence. PW-1's unrebutted testimony has established that rent was fixed at 4,000 per month.
Further, the defendant has not placed on record any notification to show that the suit property is covered by the Rent Control Act or by any slum area notification.
It is settled that mere assertion in pleadings,
without proof, cannot oust the jurisdiction of the civil court.
Once tenancy is validly terminated, the defendant's continued occupation is unauthorized, and the plaintiffs are entitled to mesne profits for use and occupation.
However, the quantum of mesne profits have to be determined on a reasonable basis.
While the plaintiffs claimed 2,000 per day (amounting to 60,000 per month), no independent market evidence was produced to substantiate this figure.
LiveLaw SC 19 and BrahmaNand Puri v NekPuri 1965 2 SCR 233 to argue that plaintiffs were required to establish title in order to be successful in a suit for possession.
In a suit between landlord and tenant, plaintiff is not required to prove title if he is able to establish landlord-tenant relationship.
Once the said relationship is established, the plaintiffs were not required to prove their ownership over the suit property.
